events.text: The creed is painted on the wall of the great hall in characters as tall as a child: STRENGTH ABOVE ALL. Before the paint is dry the first challenge is made, a disciple against an elder, in the courtyard, for the elder's seat. The whole hall comes out to watch. Nobody stops it. That is the creed.

effects.log: The disciple loses, badly, and is given the elder's respect instead of the seat. Both seem satisfied.
You fight the winner and win. Nobody in the hall doubts who leads.

events.text: You have the creed carved over the gate where every carter and farmer on the road can read it: PROTECT THE COMMON PEOPLE. An old woman from the village below stops her cart, reads it twice, and says, "We will see." She comes back a week later with a sack of rice and a complaint about bandits.

choices.text: Take the complaint first, the rice second

effects.log: Your disciples are on the bandits' trail by noon. The old woman leaves the rice anyway.
"We do not charge," you say. She looks at you as if you are very young, and leaves it anyway.

events.text: There is no banner. There is no carving over the gate. The creed is written once, small, on a plain board inside the meditation hall: THE DAO ALONE. A disciple asks what the sect will do about the quarrels of the world outside. You point at the board.

effects.log: The disciple thinks about it for a month, and then thanks you.
You explain it. It takes an afternoon. At the end the disciple understands less, and so, a little, do you.

events.text: The creed hangs in gold leaf over the counting house, not the training hall: WEALTH IS POWER. Within a month the sect owns a share in a salt boat, two teahouses and an inn on the river road. The other sects laugh at you over their empty rice jars.

effects.log: They laugh all the way to your counting house, when the harvest fails, to borrow.
You buy it. The disciples learn to count before they learn to bow. Some of them are better at it.

events.text: The creed is not on any wall. It is in a book: VENGEANCE NEVER FORGETS, written on the first page, and on every page after it a name, a date, and a wrong done to the sect. The book is empty, still. A disciple asks how long that will last.

choices.text: Say: as long as nobody wrongs us

effects.log: The disciple nods. Within the year the book has its first name.

choices.text: Write your own first enemy in it

effects.log: You write the name of the first person who ever wronged you. The disciples watch you blow on the ink.

events.text: {npc} has knocked down two of your gatekeepers to get in, and apologises to neither. "I heard the strong rise here," {he} says, wiping {his} knuckles. "I am strong." Behind {him} the gatekeepers are getting up, and they look more impressed than angry.

effects.log: {npc} kneels at last, grinning, and is given a robe two sizes too big.
{npc} goes. You suspect {he} will be back, with better manners and harder fists.

events.text: {npc} arrives with mud to the knees and a sack of rice from {his} village, which is the village's way of saying it will hold you to your creed. "They sent me to learn how to protect them," {npc} says, "because nobody else will."

choices.text: Take {him} in, and the rice to the kitchen

effects.log: {npc} eats a bowl of {his} own village's rice at your table that night, very slowly.

choices.text: Send {him} home with a promise instead

effects.log: You send {npc} home with two of your disciples to stay the winter in the village. It is not what {he} asked for.

events.text: {npc} has been sitting outside the gate for three days without asking to come in. When you finally go out, {he} asks you one question about the Dao, and it is a better question than any your disciples have asked in a year.

effects.log: {npc} stands, bows, and walks in as if {he} has always lived there.

choices.text: Answer the question and send {him} on

effects.log: You answer it. {npc} thanks you, and walks away up the mountain road, satisfied.

events.text: {npc} arrives in a hired carriage with a letter of introduction, a chest of silver from {his} family and a ledger of what the family expects in return. "Wealth is power," {he} says, with a merchant's smile. "I am told you believe it."

effects.log: The chest goes to the counting house, {npc} to the training hall. Both turn out to be useful.

choices.text: Send back the chest and keep the student

effects.log: You send back the silver. {npc} stays anyway, curious about a sect that refuses money.
{npc} bows coolly and gets back into the carriage. {His} family will remember.

events.text: {npc} is very young and very quiet and carries a name {he} will not say: the name of whoever burned {his} family's house. "Your book never forgets," {he} says. "Teach me so I do not forget either."

choices.text: Take {him} in, and the name into the book

effects.log: You write the name in the book together. {npc} watches the ink dry the way other children watch fire.

choices.text: Take {him} in, but not the name

effects.log: "Learn first," you say. "Remember later." {npc} does not like it. {He} stays.
{npc} goes without a word. Somewhere, someone has a little more time.

events.text: The elders come to you together, which they never do. The sect is soft, they say. Too many disciples who have never had to fight for their bowl of rice. They want a trial: every disciple who loses three bouts in a row goes back to the kitchens. "Strength above all," the eldest says. "You wrote it."

effects.log: The trials are brutal and fair. A third of the hall goes to the kitchens, and fights its way back out within the year.
You overrule them. The eldest bows very slowly, as if you had lost a bout yourself.

events.text: Famine in the valley. The elders want to open the sect's granary to the villages, all of it, even the seed grain for next year. "If we keep it," the eldest says, "what is the creed over the gate for? Decoration?"

effects.log: The villages eat. Next spring the sect plants late and thin, and the villages send their sons and daughters to help.
Half the granary goes out. The elders say nothing. The creed over the gate seems to look down at you.

events.text: A great house of the world outside has sent an envoy with an offer: a hundred taels a year if your sect will teach its sons. The elders advise refusing. "They do not want the Dao," says the eldest. "They want a name to put in a letter."

effects.log: The envoy leaves offended. The meditation hall is quiet again. That is worth more than a hundred taels.
The sons arrive in silk and leave within the year, having learned how to sit still for an hour. Some of them never forget it.

events.text: The elders of the counting house bring a proposal: buy up the rice of the whole province before the floods, and sell it back after. It is legal. It is very profitable. The youngest of them will not look at you while the eldest explains.

effects.log: The sect's coffers overflow. The province eats, at a price. The youngest elder resigns.

choices.text: Buy the rice, and sell it at cost

effects.log: You buy it and sell it at cost. The eldest calls it bad business. The province calls it something else.

events.text: A sect that wronged yours a generation ago is in trouble: its master dead, its halls half empty. The keepers of the book of grudges come to you with the page open. "It will never be easier," says the eldest. "The creed does not say: when convenient."

effects.log: Your disciples go down the mountain. The page is closed. It was not a great victory, and it was a complete one.
The page stays open. The eldest closes the book with a snap that you feel in your teeth.

events.text: A disciple of yours, the strongest in the hall, has beaten an elder fairly and claims the elder's seat by the creed. The elder is your oldest friend in the sect.

effects.log: Your friend steps down with a bow and moves to a smaller room. The creed holds. The friendship does, barely.

choices.text: Keep your friend in the seat

effects.log: You keep your friend where they are. The strongest disciple leaves the hall that night, and the whole sect knows why.

events.text: A rival master challenges you before your own disciples. You are tired, and wounded from last month, and could decline with honour in any other sect. Not in this one.

effects.log: You fight. You win, just, and limp back into the hall to a silence that means more than cheering.
You decline. Under a creed of strength, nobody says anything, and that is worse than anything they could say.

events.text: A lord's soldiers are burning a village for its unpaid taxes. The lord is a friend of the sect, and pays for its new roof. Your disciples are waiting for your word at the gate.

effects.log: Your disciples stop the burning. The lord withdraws his silver and his friendship. The village keeps its houses.
The smoke goes up all afternoon. Your disciples watch it from the wall, and then stop watching you.

events.text: A farmer's child has been taken by something in the forest that has already killed two hunters. Going after it means sending your best, and some of them may not come back.

effects.log: You go. The child comes home. So, after three days, do all of you.

choices.text: Post a reward for hunters instead

effects.log: Hunters go in. One comes out, without the child. The village does not send its rice to the sect again.

events.text: A powerful family offers to make your sect its own: rich patronage, a seat at its table, in return for training its guards and taking its side in its quarrels.

effects.log: You refuse. The sect stays poor and quiet and free. The meditation hall seems larger afterwards.
You accept. Within a year your disciples are breaking heads at the family's orders. Nobody meditates much any more.

events.text: Someone has insulted the sect publicly, in the market, and your disciples are furious. They want you to answer. The creed says the quarrels of the world are dust. Your own pride says otherwise.

effects.log: You let it pass. The insult is forgotten in a month. Your disciples take longer, but they learn something.
You answer it, thoroughly. The market talks of nothing else. The meditation hall stays empty for a week.

events.text: A disciple who was once a beggar asks for the sect's help: a loan to buy the land under their old street. It will never be repaid.

effects.log: You refuse it as the creed says: wealth is power, and power is not given away. The disciple understands, and does not forgive.

choices.text: Give the money as a gift

effects.log: You give it. The street has a well now. The counting house writes it down as a loss, and you as a fool.

events.text: A ruined trading house begs to sell your sect its warehouses for a tenth of their worth. It is the deal of a generation. The family will be on the street by winter.

effects.log: You buy them. The counting house cheers. The family goes north to relatives, and does not curse you, which is somehow worse.
You pay a fair price. The counting house calls it the worst deal in the sect's history. The family names a child after you.

events.text: The one whose name was first in the sect's book of grudges comes to your gate, old and alone, and asks to be forgiven before dying. The whole hall is watching.

effects.log: You close the gate. The old enemy sits outside it all night and is gone by morning. The book stays as it is.
You forgive them and strike the name from the book. Your disciples look at you as if you had torn out a page of the creed. You have.

events.text: A disciple of yours has been killed in a duel by a disciple of another sect, fairly, by every rule. The other sect offers apology and blood-money. The creed says the debt is not paid in silver.

choices.text: Refuse the money and demand the duellist

effects.log: You refuse the money. In the end the duellist comes to your gate and fights again, and loses. The book closes the page.
You accept it. Your disciples stop writing in the book. Some of them stop believing in it.

events.text: That night someone scrapes a line through the creed on the wall of the hall: one long scratch, through every character, with the point of a knife. In the morning a disciple is already painting it over. Nobody asks who did it. Everyone knows why.

effects.log: You take the brush from the disciple and paint it over yourself. It does not quite hide the scratch.
You leave it. Let them see what you did. The heart does not get lighter for it.

events.text: The disciples no longer recite the creed at the morning gathering. They mumble it, or skip it, or say it very loudly with a look at you that is not quite insolence. The sect is still yours. Its creed seems less sure.

choices.text: Recite it yourself, alone, every morning

effects.log: You stand alone in the cold courtyard and say it. Some mornings, now, one or two say it with you.
The morning gathering is quieter. You sleep a little worse.

events.text: An old disciple, nearly blind now, asks to be led to the wall of the hall so that they can touch the creed. They run their fingers over the characters one by one and nod as if the wall had answered a question.

effects.log: You lead them there every morning until their death. The wall is worn smooth in one place.
"Still true," the old disciple says. That is all.

events.text: A traveller asks your gatekeeper what kind of sect this is, and the gatekeeper answers with the creed, word for word, without stopping to think. You overhear it, and find that you are proud.

effects.log: The gatekeeper is moved inside, protesting. The new gatekeeper learns the creed in a day.
You walk on. Some things are better left unpraised, so they stay true.

events.text: The creed is gone from the wall. Someone has taken it down in the night, board and all, and carried it out of the gate. The pale space where it hung is the first thing every disciple sees in the morning.

effects.log: You leave it empty. It is more honest than anything you could hang there.

choices.text: Promise the hall you will earn it back

effects.log: You make the promise aloud. Promises in this hall are remembered now. You will be held to it.

events.text: The elders bring you the founder's creed on its board, wrapped in silk, the way it has been brought to every leader of the sect. "Read it as it was written," the eldest says, "or read it as you are. Either way the sect will follow. Only do not pretend."

choices.text: Swear to it as it was written

effects.log: You swear to it word for word. The eldest nods once and does not smile, which from him is joy.
You read it aloud, and the words mean something different in your mouth. The elders hear it. The young ones lean in.

events.text: The founder's creed hangs over your head every time you sit in the seat. The old disciples quote it at you. The young ones ask what it means now, in a world the founder never saw.

choices.text: Tell them: what it always meant

effects.log: Some of the young ones look disappointed. The old ones look as if they can breathe again.

choices.text: Tell them: what we need it to mean

effects.log: You give them a new reading. It is clever and it is useful and the founder would not have recognised it.

events.text: The elders of the sect you took in kneel in your hall in their old colours. They have lost their gate, their name and half their people. They ask to keep one thing: their own creed, beside yours.

effects.log: They bow and take off their old colours. Some of them weep. Your creed stays as it was.

choices.text: Read yours so theirs fits inside it

effects.log: You read your creed in a way that makes room for theirs. Both halls cheer. Your oldest disciples look at the wall a long time.

events.text: The absorbed sect's disciples recite their old creed at night in their dormitory, quietly, when they think no one is listening. Your own disciples are listening, and want you to stop it.

effects.log: It stops. The dormitory is silent at night now. Silence is not the same as loyalty.

choices.text: Join them one night and listen

effects.log: You listen. Their creed is not so far from yours, said a certain way. You begin to say yours that way.

events.text: The creed on the wall is the same characters. It is not the same creed. The young disciples say it the new way, fast and sure. The old ones say it the old way, slowly, and their voices do not quite match.

choices.text: Say it the new way, loudly

effects.log: Your voice carries over theirs. The old way goes quiet, mostly.
Two creeds in one hall. It is untidy. It may be the truest thing about the sect.

events.text: Your disciples come back from the war with the throne's thanks and fewer of their number. In the hall they stand under the creed and are counted, and the count is said aloud, and then the creed. The two sound like one thing.

choices.text: Read the names of the dead

effects.log: You read every name. The creed was kept, and it cost exactly this much. The sect remembers both.
The feast is loud and long and the empty places at the table are kept full of wine.

events.text: The war went on beyond your gate and your sect's side in it was not the creed's. In the hall, under the wall where it is written, a disciple stands up at the evening meal and asks you why. Everyone stops eating.

effects.log: You answer. It is a good answer, as answers go. The disciple sits down. The question does not.
The disciple sits. The question is asked again the next night, by someone else.
